A progressive unfolding correction shows that the site-mean direction has the highest precision pa- rameter at 103.6% unfolding (with 95% uncertainties ranging from 100.4% to 107.3%) (Watson and Enkin, 1993). Furthermore, the re- versal test is positive at the 95% conﬁdence level (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990)( Fig. 7, Table 1). Therefore, we conclude that the group Mean-D direction indicates a pre-folding origin; we attribute this folding to the Lhasa-Qiangtang collision, which occurred in Late Jurassic–Early Cretaceous time (Kapp et al., 2007). We conclude that the ChRM directions of the 29 groups that deﬁne Mean-D record a primary thermoremanence. We do not ob- serve any paleomagnetic, rock magnetic, or petrographic evidence that suggests the ChRM directions are biased by unremoved over- prints. These rocks are dated to 204–213 Ma. Progressive thermal or alternating ﬁeld demagnetization successfully isolated stable characteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRM) that pass both the fold and reversal tests, consistent with a primary magnetization. These are the ﬁrst volcanic- based paleomagnetic results from pre-Cretaceous rocks of the Qiangtang block that appear to average secular variation well enough to yield a reliable paleolatitude estimate. Based on our new paleomagnetic data from Upper Triassic lavas, we conclude that the Late Triassic pole of the Qiangtang block was located at 64.0◦N, 174.7◦E, with A95 = 6.6◦ (N = 29). Based on our new paleomagnetic data from Upper Triassic lavas, we conclude that the Late Triassic pole of the Qiangtang block was located at 64.0◦N, 174.7◦E, with A95 = 6.6◦ (N = 29). We compile published paleomagnetic data from the Qiangtang block to calculate a Late Triassic latitude for the Qiangtang block at 31.7 ± 3.0◦N. The central Paleo-Tethys Ocean basin was located between the North China (NCB) and Tarim blocks to the north and the Qiangtang block to the south during Late Paleozoic–Early Mesozoic. A comparison of published Early Triassic paleopole from the Qiangtang block with the coeval paleopoles from the NCB and Tarim indicates that the Paleo-Tethys Ocean could not have closed during the Early Triassic and that its width was approximately ∼32–38◦ latitude (∼3500–4200 km). However, the comparison of our new combined Late Triassic paleomagnetic result with the Late Triassic poles of the NCB and Tarim, as well as numerous geological observations, indicates that the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean at the longitude of the Qiangtang block most likely occurred during the Late Triassic. © 2015 Elsevier B.V. Paleomagnetic data from Late Triassic rocks of the Qiangtang block are limited, such that paleomagnetism has not been used with rigor to address the timing of the closure of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean; these data could, however, provide independent constraints on this collision history. For example, published paleomagnetic data from Late Triassic volcanic and sedimentary rocks yield pa- leolatitude estimates that range from 24◦S to 30◦N (Cheng, 2012; Lin and Watts, 1988; Song et al., 2012; Ye and Li, 1987). Song et al. (2012) obtained two Late Triassic paleopoles from the Late Triassic sedimentary rocks in the central Qiangtang block: one at 59.2◦N, 179.2◦E, with A95 = 4.1◦, and the other at 65.1◦N, 184.4◦E, with A95 = 3.7◦; data for both poles pass fold and re- versal tests. We note, however, that paleomagnetic results from Cenozoic sediments in Asia record inclinations that are 10–30◦ more shallow than coeval volcanic rocks or predicted from the coeval Eurasia reference poles (e.g., Dupont-Nivet et al., 2010; Lippert et al., 2011), probably due to deposition and compaction of sediments (Kodama, 2012)o r non-dipole ﬁeld effects (Si and Voo, 2001). Bearing in mind the importance of further investigation, the red beds of the Phuquoc–Kampot Som Basin were chosen for a new paleomagnetic study. The basin is located to the south of the Khorat Basin and occupies a central part of the Indochina Block. According to some researchers (Lacassin et al., 1997; Fyhn et al., 2010; Morley, 2012), these two basins remained a part of a con- tinuous large basin prior to its splitting by left-lateral tectonic movements along the Wang Chao Fault (Mae-Ping shear zone). To document the tectonic movement in the southernmost region of the Indochina Peninsula with respect to its main northern part, we sampled late Jurassic to early Cretaceous red beds from the Si- hanoukville (11.5◦N, 103.7◦E) and Koah Kong (11.6◦N, 103.5◦E) ar- eas in southwestern Cambodia, southwest of the Cardamom Moun- tains. 2. Geological setting and sampling The Indochina Peninsula comprises a collage of continental blocks that include the Lanping-Simao Terrane and Indochina Block (Ferrari et al., 2008; Metcalfe, 2011). A widespread presence of Late Jurassic to Cretaceous sedimentary rocks characterizes the Mesozoic strata in the blocks. DISCUSSION The component analysis of the natural remanent magnetization of the Devonian and Carboniferous sed- imentary rocks of Spitsbergen revealed two-component Jn in all samples. Component A, isolated in a wide tem- perature interval (100–350°С, 100–450°С, and 100– 550°С), is most likely to be related to both the viscous magnetization of the rocks by the Cenozoic geomag- netic field and the chemical alterations caused by weathering. The second high-temperature component in most of the sections is bipolar and pre-folding. The zones of normal and reverse polarity identified in our study for the Fiskeklofta Formation are coherent with the results obtained by other authors (Kolesov , 1985; Pogarskaya and Gurevich, 1988). The positive reversals tests and the reasonable correspondence between the locations of the zones of normal and reverse polarity revealed in our study and the general magnetostrati- graphic scale (Fig. 4) also support the old age of the iso- lated characteristic components of Jn. The Middle Carboniferous rocks (the lower part of Bashkirian stage C2b) were sampled from the south- western slope of Mt Pyramiden from a height of 370 m upwards (Fig. 1, sampling locality 10). The rocks are represented by limestones, brown red sandstones with interbeds of conglomerates. Nineteen stratigraphic lev- els were sampled with a step of 2–10 m; 19 hand sam- ples (50 specimens) were studied. The paleomagnetic measurements and processing of the obtained results followed a common procedure ( Paleomagnitologiya, 1982). Thermal demagnetization was carried out using the instruments placed in a five- layer permalloy shield (original design by All Russia Petroleum Research Exploration Institute (VNIGRI)) and TD48 thermal demagnetizer (US). The natural remanent magnetization Jn and its values during step- wise demagnetization were measured by the JR-4 and JR-5 Agico magnetometers (Czech Republic). A part of the samples was studied in the laboratory at Lund Uni- versity (Sweden) using the Schonstedt TSD-1 furnace; the measurements were conducted by the 2G cryogenic magnetometer. The paleogeographic reconstructions were made by the GMAP program (T orsvik and Smethurst, 1999). In the data processing, the statistics were estimated at the hand-sample level. DISCUSSION The component analysis of the natural remanent magnetization of the Devonian and Carboniferous sed- imentary rocks of Spitsbergen revealed two-component Jn in all samples. Component A, isolated in a wide tem- perature interval (100–350°С, 100–450°С, and 100– 550°С), is most likely to be related to both the viscous magnetization of the rocks by the Cenozoic geomag- netic field and the chemical alterations caused by weathering. The second high-temperature component in most of the sections is bipolar and pre-folding. The zones of normal and reverse polarity identified in our study for the Fiskeklofta Formation are coherent with the results obtained by other authors (Kolesov , 1985; Pogarskaya and Gurevich, 1988). The positive reversals tests and the reasonable correspondence between the locations of the zones of normal and reverse polarity revealed in our study and the general magnetostrati- graphic scale (Fig. 4) also support the old age of the iso- lated characteristic components of Jn. In this paper, we present the paleomagnetic results determined from the Devonian and Carboniferous sections of the Island of Spitsbergen. The collection of Devonian and Car- boniferous rock samples was obtained during the field campaigns of 1986 and 1987. The first results of study- ing this collection were published in (Pogarskaya and Gurevich, 1988; Iosifidi et al., 2007). THE OBJECTS OF STUDY AND PROCEDURE OF ANALYSIS Devonian sediments. Liefdefjorden. On the northern coast of Liefdefjorden (Mt. Pteraspistoppen), at the fjord’s head, the rocks of Early Devonian age (lower portion of Fraenkelryggen Formation, Red Bay series) were sampled from the coastal cliffs (Fig. 1, sampling locality 1). The rocks are represented by the alternation of brown red, inequigranular, often cross-bedded sand- stones and siltstones (Murashov and Mokin, 1976; Stratigraficheskii…, 1990); these rocks correspond to the tops of the Lochkovian stage, D1l. The Fraenkel- ryggen Formation has an apparent thickness of 600 m. In this paper, we present the results of studying its lower part, from which 41 hand sample were acquired with a sampling step of 2–3 m; the total thickness of the stud- ied interval is 200 m (in the upper 80 m, the samples were taken every 5–10 m). DISCUSSION The component analysis of the natural remanent magnetization of the Devonian and Carboniferous sed- imentary rocks of Spitsbergen revealed two-component Jn in all samples. Component A, isolated in a wide tem- perature interval (100–350°С, 100–450°С, and 100– 550°С), is most likely to be related to both the viscous magnetization of the rocks by the Cenozoic geomag- netic field and the chemical alterations caused by weathering. The second high-temperature component in most of the sections is bipolar and pre-folding. The zones of normal and reverse polarity identified in our study for the Fiskeklofta Formation are coherent with the results obtained by other authors (Kolesov , 1985; Pogarskaya and Gurevich, 1988). The positive reversals tests and the reasonable correspondence between the locations of the zones of normal and reverse polarity revealed in our study and the general magnetostrati- graphic scale (Fig. 4) also support the old age of the iso- lated characteristic components of Jn. This sense of tectonic mobility does not support the hypothesis about transformation from Pangea ‘B’ to Pangea ‘A’ along an intra-Pangea dextral megashear during the Permian. Europe can be older than pre- viously assumed. If so, then overlap of Gondwana’ s and Laurus- sia’ s parts of the Early Permian Pangea ‘A’ could be additionally reduced. The palaeomagnetic data from the Sudetes (Nawrocki 1998) and some geological observations performed in the southern part of Germany (Mattern 2001) indicate that during the Permian the NW– SE trending faults recorded rather a sinistral sense of the tectonic transport. STUDY AREA AND PREVIOUS P ALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS The border zone of the Brunosilesia and Ma /suppresslopolska terranes is deﬁned by a narrow fault zone ‘Cracow-Lubliniec’ that probably represents a segment of much larger, transcontinental tectonic line ‘Cracow-Hamburg’ (Fig. 1a;˙Zaba 1999). This zone has Proterezoic foundations, and was active from earliest Palaeozoic through to Cenozoic times. The effects of polyphase activity of this fault control the structural features of the whole zone including areas with igneous rocks of the Krzeszowice region, where vertical faulting, related to the tectonic activity of the deep substratum, led to the formation of numerous fault macroblocks (op. cit.). The Late Palaeozoic volcanic rocks of the Krzeszowice region are exposed over an area of approximately 200 km 2 about 20 km west of Cracow in Southern Poland (Fig. 1b). Composition of the volcanic rocks ranges from basaltic trachyandesites to rhyodacites with mi- nor andesites and lamprophyres (Czerny & Muszy´nski 1997, 2000). Basaltic trachyandesites form several lava ﬂows intercalated with pyroclastics and erupted along SE–NW trending faults bordering Nieporaz-Brod/suppressla graben (Fig. 1b). The Late Palaeozoic volcanic rocks of the Krzeszowice region are exposed over an area of approximately 200 km 2 about 20 km west of Cracow in Southern Poland (Fig. 1b). Composition of the volcanic rocks ranges from basaltic trachyandesites to rhyodacites with mi- nor andesites and lamprophyres (Czerny & Muszy´nski 1997, 2000). Basaltic trachyandesites form several lava ﬂows intercalated with pyroclastics and erupted along SE–NW trending faults bordering Nieporaz-Brod/suppressla graben (Fig. 1b). Sporadically basaltic rocks form small intrusions, for example, a sill in Nied´zwiedzia G´ora. Rhyo- dacites intruded at shallow levels forming predominantly laccoliths and have been encountered in Zalas-Orlej, Mikinia and Dubie vicin- ity. Felsic tuffs outcrop in the area of Filipowice. This zone has Proterezoic foundations, and was active from earliest Palaeozoic through to Cenozoic times. section_candidates.excerpt: Volcanics, Hiltaba Suite Granitoids, Alice Springs Orogeny, paleomagnetism, ﬁssion track dating INTRODUCTION The *1590 Ma Gawler Range Volcanics (GRV) and the 1595–1575 Ma Hiltaba Suite Granitoids (HSG) outcrop in the central Gawler Craton of South Australia. They produce characteristic, although quite distinctive, mag- netic anomalies and can be easily mapped beneath cover. The volcanics typically produce very active magnetic patterns, while the patterns above granitoids range from subdued to remarkably ﬂat and smooth. The HSG and GRV can be subdivided into two types, each correlated with a distinctive mineral association. The more oxidised members are of the Roxby Downs-type and are associated with Fe-oxide-Cu–Au mineralisation, while the less oxidised Kokatha-types are associated with vein Au ( +Sn+Ag) mineralisation (Budd et al . 1998). Here we report magnetic properties of the Hiltaba Suite Granitoids and the Gawler Range Volcanics. Magnetic remanences and susceptibilities of samples were measured to characterise the different assem- blages and assist mineral exploration and geological interpretation of magnetic surveys over the Gawler Craton. section_candidates.excerpt: ure sug- gests a north-dipping subduction ( Buckman and Aitchison, 2004 ). This subduction zone might extent to the west into Kazakhstan. Its strike becomes progressively rotated by 180 in Central Kazakh- stan and thus connects to the North Tian Shan subduction zone (Fig. 1). This horseshoe shape corresponds to the Devonian to Car- boniferous Kazakh orocline ( Sengor and Natalin, 1996; Abrajevitch et al., 2007 ). Post-collisional magmatic rocks cross-cut the accre- tionary complex ( Chen and Jahn, 2004; Han et al., 2006; Geng et al., 2009 ), and Permian continental deposits unconformably overlie Carboniferous turbidites. Ductile to brittle deformation oc- curs along SW–NE trending sinistral faults, like Darbut Fault. Since the Paleozoic, intracontinental basins, like Junggar were ﬁlled by Mesozoic and Cenozoic sedimentary rocks covering the Paleozoic basement. Active top-to-the SE thrusting allows the Paleozoic basement of the West Junggar Mountains to be locally exposed along the Darbut Fault or the Uhre thrust near Karamay City. 2.4. Recent U/Pb datings of zir- con from altered tuffs from Baogutu Formation yield a Visean age (between 343 and 328 Ma; Wang and Zhu, 2007 ; An and Zhu, 2009) and Late Carboniferous detrital zircons were found in similar formation near Karamay ( Zhang, 2009 ). The negative fold test with a decrease of the precision parameter after bedding corrections reveals a remagnetization of these Car- boniferous rocks ( Table 1). The observation of solely reverse polar- ities for this long Carboniferous sedimentary series may indicate that the age of the remanence is probably not older than the lower limit of the Kiaman superchron (i.e. 325 Ma; Hounslow et al., 2004). Introduction [2] The study reported here is a follow up to work reported on equatorial lavas from Ecuador, which suggested a contribution from a quadrupole of about 5% to the time ‐averaged field [ Opdyke et al. , 2006]. The present study is designed to see if this result can be replicated at another equatorial site. Therefore field collecting began in August 2006 in the Loiyangalani and Mount Kenya regions of Kenya (Figure 1). Abstract The Qaidam basin is the largest topographic depression inside the Tibetan Plateau and it is a key factor to understanding the Cenozoic evolution of the northern Tibetan Plateau. Paleomagnetic data was obtained from the middle to late Eocene Xiaganchaigou Formation and the early to middle Miocene Xiayoushashan Formation from seven localities. The paleomagnetic results indicate that the Qaidam basin has not undergone obvious basin-scale vertical axis rotation with respect to the Eurasia Plate since the Eocene. Local clockwise rotation took place only at a few special locations along the northern margin of the Qaidam basin. The uniform paleomagnetic results at different localities support that the Qaidam basin is a relatively rigid block. Regional paleomagnetic and geodetic observations also suggest that crust south of the Kunlun fault moves eastward faster than crust north of the Kunlun fault. 1. Introduction The Qaidam basin is the largest Cenozoic basin in the Tibetan Plateau. Located within the northern Tibetan plateau region, the evolution of the Qaidam basin has attracted researchers’ widespread attention. The Qai- dam basin is bounded by three huge fault zones: the Eastern Kunlun Fault Zone to the south, the Altyn Tagh Fault Zone to the northwest and the Qilian Shan-Nan Shan Thrust Zone

went intense compressional deformation and attendant crustal thickening. Many researchers have attained a series of meaningful results within the Qaidam basin to reveal its geologic his- tory [Wang and Coward, 1993; Metivier et al., 1998; Robinson et al., 2003; Wang et al., 2004; Zhu et al., 2006; Yin et al., 2007, 2008a, 2008b;Kent-Corson et al., 2009; Kapp et al., 2011; Heermance et al., 2013; Song et al., 2013]. Moreover, an array of magnetostratigraphic and environmental magnetic work has also been conducted [Sun et al., 2005; Fang et al., 2007; Lu et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2012a, 2012b;Chang et al., 2012]. Speciﬁcally, some tec- tonic paleomagnetic results within the Qaidam basin have been published [Chen et al., 2002; Dupont-Nivet et al., 2002]. Despite these studies, there is still some disagreement concerning the timing, magnitude, and distribution of vertical axis rotations within the Qaidam basin. The mean paleomagnetic declinations at locations in central Qaidam basin indicate no vertical axis rotation since the Oligocene [Dupont-Nivet et al., 2002]. In contrast, based on results from two other localities within the northern Qaidam basin,Chen et al. [2002] concluded that sinistral lateral-slip on the Altyn Tagh Fault was accommodated by approximately 20 of clockwise rotation of the Qai

rotations within the Qaidam basin. The mean paleomagnetic declinations at locations in central Qaidam basin indicate no vertical axis rotation since the Oligocene [Dupont-Nivet et al., 2002]. In contrast, based on results from two other localities within the northern Qaidam basin,Chen et al. [2002] concluded that sinistral lateral-slip on the Altyn Tagh Fault was accommodated by approximately 20 of clockwise rotation of the Qai- dam basin at the end of or after the Oligocene. To resolve this debate effectively, we conduct a paleomagnetic study of coeval Cenozoic rocks widespread in the Qaidam basin: the middle to upper Eocene Xiaganchaigou Formation and the lower to middle Miocene Xiayoushashan Formation. We sampled these units at seven local- ities throughout the basin (Xichagou, Gansen, Eboliang, Heishiqiu, Lulehe, Kushuiqua n ,a n dG a h a i ) ,w h i c hs h o u l d provide an ideal opportunity to characterize the distribution of vertical axis rotations throughout the Qaidam basin. - sis reveals three components of Natural Remanent Magnetization (NRM). Heating to 808C removes a remanent magnetization parallel to the present-day ﬁeld, which is interpreted as a viscous overprint. An intermediate unblocking temperature component is removed by heating to 450 8C; this direction is always of normal polarity and is identical to a regional overprint imparted during the Early Jurassic emplacement of the Karoo Large Igneous Province. A high-temperature component isolated above 450 8C is of dual polar- ity and is interpreted as primary on the basis of a positive reversals test. The virtual geomagnetic pole posi- tion for the Abrahamskraal Formation computed from the average high-temperature characteristic remanent magnetization direction is in agreement with the late Permian directions for stable Gondwana and with previous results from the lowermost Abrahamskraal Formation and Waterford Formation at the Ouberg Pass section. The predominantly normal polarity of this magnetization is in agreement with either a middle-late Lopingian age (ca. 254–256 Ma) or a late Guadalupian age (ca. 262 Ma) according to the global geomagnetic polarity time scale. et al ., 1983; Hansma et al ., 2015]. The base of the Karoo Supergroup is deﬁned by glacio-marine diamictites of the Permian-Carboniferous Dwyka Group, which is overlain by deep water turbidites to ﬂuvio-deltaic sediments of the Ecca Group. The Beaufort Group conformably overlies the Ecca Group, and is dominated by ﬂuvial sandstones and mudstones [e.g., Smith et al ., 1993; Catuneanu et al ., 2005]. The base of the Beaufort Group marks the sedimentologic shift from deep water, marine, and deltaic facies to ﬂuvial systems with episodic subaerial exposure, marked in the ﬁeld by the lowermost occurrences of reddish, oxidized mudstones. The Abrahamskraal Formation is the lowest unit of the Beaufort Group, and this formation comprises a k m thick sequence of mudstones and sandstones [ Day and Rubidge , 2014]. The lithostratigraphic divisions of the Karoo Group are well-deﬁned, but the absolute age information is lim- ited and some degree of diachronism is expected. Biostratigraphic ages for the Karoo Supergroup are based upon palynologic and faunal vertebrate records. The Ecca Group hosts a Early to Middle Permian palyno- logic assemblage [ Anderson, 1977; Falcon, 1989; Barbolini, 2014; Ruckwied et al ., 2014], with the occurrence of Mesosaurus fossils in the distinctive Whitehill Format

on palynologic and faunal vertebrate records. The Ecca Group hosts a Early to Middle Permian palyno- logic assemblage [ Anderson, 1977; Falcon, 1989; Barbolini, 2014; Ruckwied et al ., 2014], with the occurrence of Mesosaurus fossils in the distinctive Whitehill Formation [ von Huene, 1940] in the lower Ecca Group estab- lishing a clear tie-point to the ca. 278 Ma Irat ı Formation of the Passa Dois Group in the Paran a Basin of South America [ Santos et al ., 2006]. The contact between the Ecca Group and the Beaufort Group is deﬁned as the boundary between the Eodicynodon and Tapinocephalus assemblage zones [ Rubidge et al ., 1999]. The Abrahamskraal Formation lies within the Tapinocephalus zone [ van der Walt et al ., 2010; Day and Rubidge , 2014; Jirah and Rubidge , 2014]. The upper Beaufort Group is interpreted to preserve a record of the Permian-Triassic mass extinction, which is represented by the boundary between Dyconodon and Lystrosaurus zones [e.g., Maxwell, 1992; Botha and Smith, 2007; cf. Gastaldo et al., 2015]. To complement this biostratigraphic database, thereis a growing body of U-Pb zircon ages from volcanic ash- beds that are preserved in the Karoo Supergroup. rom volcanic ash- beds that are preserved in the Karoo Supergroup. The Dwyka Group is considered to be about 302–290 Ma in age based on ID-TIMS analysis of zircon [Bangert et al., 1999]. Studies of the overlying Ecca Group were carried out using the U-Pb SHRIMP method on zircons from volcanic ashes [Fildani et al., 2007, 2009; McKay et al., 2015]. These authors jointly interpret an age range of 252– 276 Ma for deposition of the Ecca Group. However, the younger portion of this age range contradicts the 262–268 Ma age determined for the uppermost Ecca Group and basal Beaufort Group by Lanci et al. Here we present paleomagnetic data from 13 late Variscan dykes from Sardinia ranging in age from 298 6 5 to 270 6 10 Ma. The dykes can be grouped on the basis of their different directions in strike in a northern, a central-eastern and a south-eastern province. Paleomagnetic component directions have been obtained using thermal and alternating ﬁeld demagnetiza- tion techniques, which give reproducible results. The paleomagnetic mean directions differ signiﬁcantly between northern Sardinia and south-eastern and central-eastern Sardinia, the latter two regions yieldin

l., 2011], can no longer be maintained for pre-Jurassic times. This opens the possibility—explored in this paper—that these dykes were variably rotated shortly after emplacement and could represent evidence of Permian shearing between Laurasia and Gondwana. The aim of this study is therefore to investigate whether the different strike directions of Sardinian dykes are of primary or secondary origin in order to quantify internal rotations within Sardinia and their implica- tions for the inferred Pangea megashear system. 2. from 298 6 5 to 270 6 10 Ma. The dykes can be grouped on the basis of their different directions in strike in a northern, a central-eastern and a south-eastern province. Paleomagnetic component directions have been obtained using thermal and alternating ﬁeld demagnetiza- tion techniques, which give reproducible results. The paleomagnetic mean directions differ signiﬁcantly between northern Sardinia and south-eastern and central-eastern Sardinia, the latter two regions yielding statistically similar paleomagnetic mean directions. These results indicate that Sardinia fragmented into two, arguably three, crustal blocks after emplacement of the dykes, which experienced differential relative rotations, as is also indicated by the differences in overall strike directions. The determination of timing, sense, and magnitude of these rotations has major implications for the reconstruction of the geodynamic evolution of the region in post-Carboniferous times. We argue that the observed block rotations occurred during the Permian as the result of post-Variscan intra-Pangea mobility possibly related to the transforma- tion of an Early Permian Pangea B to a Late Permian Pangea A. 1. Introduction It has been previously observed that the use of paleomagnetic data to reconstruct Pangea A (Wegenerian Pangea) in the Early Permian results in a signiﬁcant continental overlap of Laurasia and Gondwana, and that one of the options to overcome this problem is to choose an alternative conﬁguration known as Pangea B, characterized by the southern continents of Gondwana located further to the East with respect to Laurasia [Irving, 1977; Morel and Irving , 1981; Muttoni et al ., 2003; see Aubele et al . [2012] and Domeier et al . [2012] for a discussion of the Pangea controversy). However, since there is no reason to doubt that the opening of the Atlantic Ocean and the dispersal of Pangea started from a Pangea A conﬁguration, a large dextral mega- shear zone between Laurasia and Gondwana becomes a necessary feature for the transformation from a postulated Pangea B to a widely accepted Pangea A conﬁguration (Figure 1). from 298 6 5 to 270 6 10 Ma. The dykes can be grouped on the basis of their different directions in strike in a northern, a central-eastern and a south-eastern province. Paleomagnetic component directions have been obtained using thermal and alternating ﬁeld demagnetiza- tion techniques, which give reproducible results. The paleomagnetic mean directions differ signiﬁcantly between northern Sardinia and south-eastern and central-eastern Sardinia, the latter two regions yielding statistically similar paleomagnetic mean directions. These results indicate that Sardinia fragmented into two, arguably three, crustal blocks after emplacement of the dykes, which experienced differential relative rotations, as is also indicated by the differences in overall strike directions. The determination of timing, sense, and magnitude of these rotations has major implications for the reconstruction of the geodynamic evolution of the region in post-Carboniferous times. We argue that the observed block rotations occurred during the Permian as the result of post-Variscan intra-Pangea mobility possibly related to the transforma- tion of an Early Permian Pangea B to a Late Permian Pangea A. 1. [2012] and Domeier et al . [2012] for a discussion of the Pangea controversy). However, since there is no reason to doubt that the opening of the Atlantic Ocean and the dispersal of Pangea started from a Pangea A conﬁguration, a large dextral mega- shear zone between Laurasia and Gondwana becomes a necessary feature for the transformation from a postulated Pangea B to a widely accepted Pangea A conﬁguration (Figure 1). Based on a variety of geologi- cal evidence [e.g., Arthaud and Matte , 1977; Burg et al ., 1994; Stampﬂi, 2001; Casini et al ., 2012], this tectonic zone, if real, is expected to lie within the Mediterranean realm in southern Europe and/or northern Africa. [2003] constrain the timing of transform motion to a 0 Ma interval during mid-Permian times, requiring an average relative plate velocity of 5 cm/yr. These results indicate that Sardinia fragmented into two, arguably three, crustal blocks after emplacement of the dykes, which experienced differential relative rotations, as is also indicated by the differences in overall strike directions. The determination of timing, sense, and magnitude of these rotations has major implications for the reconstruction of the geodynamic evolution of the region in post-Carboniferous times. We argue that the observed block rotations occurred during the Permian as the result of post-Variscan intra-Pangea mobility possibly related to the transforma- tion of an Early Permian Pangea B to a Late Permian Pangea A. 1. A combined geochemical and magnetostrati- graphic study was carried out at Yanyuan in the inner zone of the ELIP. Geochemical results indicate that the basalts are low ‐Ti (LT) basalts (Ti/Y ∼ 484.2–511.4) in the Luomapu section and high ‐Ti (HT) basalts (Ti/Y ∼ 558.2–658.9) in the Gongmushan section. Systematic paleomagnetic sampling and stepwise ther- mal demagnetization demonstrate that the higher temperature component shows two distinct characteristic remanent magnetizations with northeasterly upward and SWW downward directions. These results indicate a simple magnetostratigraphic normal and reversed polarity pattern from the lower and upper parts of the section, respectively. By comparing with available magnetostratigraphic and paleomagnetic data carried out in the ELIP, these results imply that the eruption of the Emeishan basalts can be divided into early (normal polarity subchron) and late (reversal subchron) stages. The early stage included LT basalts in the inner zone and most of the HT basalts in the intermediate and outer zones, and the late stage contained a part of LT and HT basalts in the upper parts of the sections in the inner zone and a few in the intermediate zone of the ELIP. Nanjing 210093, China [1] Temporal and spatial variations of high and low contents of Ti basalts in the Permian Emeishan large igneous province (ELIP) of southwest China and Vietnam are crucial for modeling of continental basalt formation and the nature of mantle ‐lithosphere interaction. A combined geochemical and magnetostrati- graphic study was carried out at Yanyuan in the inner zone of the ELIP. Geochemical results indicate that the basalts are low ‐Ti (LT) basalts (Ti/Y ∼ 484.2–511.4) in the Luomapu section and high ‐Ti (HT) basalts (Ti/Y ∼ 558.2–658.9) in the Gongmushan section. Systematic paleomagnetic sampling and stepwise ther- mal demagnetization demonstrate that the higher temperature component shows two distinct characteristic remanent magnetizations with northeasterly upward and SWW downward directions. These results indicate a simple magnetostratigraphic normal and reversed polarity pattern from the lower and upper parts of the section, respectively. By comparing with available magnetostratigraphic and paleomagnetic data carried out in the ELIP, these results imply that the eruption of the Emeishan basalts can be divided into early (normal polarity subchron) and late (reversal subchron) stages. The early stage included LT basalts in the inner zone and most of the HT basalts in th

eomagnetic sampling and stepwise ther- mal demagnetization demonstrate that the higher temperature component shows two distinct characteristic remanent magnetizations with northeasterly upward and SWW downward directions. These results indicate a simple magnetostratigraphic normal and reversed polarity pattern from the lower and upper parts of the section, respectively. By comparing with available magnetostratigraphic and paleomagnetic data carried out in the ELIP, these results imply that the eruption of the Emeishan basalts can be divided into early (normal polarity subchron) and late (reversal subchron) stages. The early stage included LT basalts in the inner zone and most of the HT basalts in the intermediate and outer zones, and the late stage contained a part of LT and HT basalts in the upper parts of the sections in the inner zone and a few in the intermediate zone of the ELIP. Correlating with available Middle ‐Late Permian magnetostratigraphy and the Permian magnetic time scale, the new magnetic polarity sequence result suggests that the ELIP formed over a very short time interval (<1 Myr).
